comparisons.interpretation: Both affirm broad access to healthcare: Sanders places healthcare for all within a progressive economic agenda, while Clinton calls affordable healthcare a human right. This goal agreement does not establish identical financing models.

Sanders explicitly names tuition-free and debt-free college; Clinton's issue summary emphasizes removing cost and debt barriers. The summary alone does not prove Clinton opposed free tuition or establish all eligibility details.

Sanders proposes a national single-payer program, while Biden proposes an optional public insurance plan building on the ACA and retaining private coverage. These are different stated coverage approaches; the source records their own plans rather than imputing the DNC platform to either.

Sanders names a national single-payer system; Klobuchar presents a public option expanding Medicare or Medicaid as the quickest route to universal coverage. Their shared access goal does not erase that institutional distinction.

Sanders proposes a national single-payer program. Buttigieg proposes an exchange-based public option as a pathway toward Medicare for All. This distinguishes implementation strategy without treating the longer-term goal as opposed.

Both platforms explicitly support Medicare for All. Sanders gives the national insurance design in this section; Warren names it among investments funded by economic reform. The shared named proposal does not establish identical financing or transition details.

Both use single-payer terminology. Gabbard expressly retains a private-insurance choice in the surrounding sentence; the short Sanders excerpt alone is not proof about every supplemental private-insurance arrangement, so no blanket contradiction is asserted.
Sanders specifies single-payer financing, while Delaney's retained issue list commits to universal health care without giving that mechanism in the quoted line. Missing detail is not opposition.

The selected Sanders passage names national rent regulation; Warren's passage names housing investment. Both full sources address affordability and investment, so these are nonexclusive emphases, not evidence of opposed housing agendas.

Sanders states a universal tuition/debt-free public-college guarantee; Buttigieg's paragraph specifies free tuition for lower- and middle-income families with aid measures. The excerpt does not establish all higher-income rules or opposition to a universal plan.

Sanders' selected passage states the renewable-energy goal; Buttigieg's passage names a carbon tax-and-dividend among Green New Deal tools. A goal and a tool can coexist and are not coded as disagreement.
Sanders' selected passage emphasizes a renewable-energy endpoint while Delaney names carbon taxation. These observations do not establish that either opposes the other's instrument.
